world.bio: I'm from Rochdale and I spent twenty-eight years at a dye works matching colours by eye, first as a learner, then as a lab hand, and finally as the senior colour matcher. The works closed last month. I'm fifty-eight, I have a mortgage that is nearly paid, a wife who wants to move to the coast, and a dog called Biscuit who doesn't care about any of it. I still can't walk past a paint chart in a shop without squinting at it.
skills_assets: Twenty-eight years of industrial dyeing and colour matching on wool, polyester, cotton and blends
Senior colour matcher at the works: matched shades by eye within the batch tolerance, a result the spectrophotometer agreed with
Knowledge of dye chemistry: reactive, disperse and acid dyes, mordants, pH control, liquor ratios, fixing agents
Recipes in my head and in a battered notebook for about 400 shades the works ran regularly
A good network of people in the north west textile trade, most of them now retired or laid off
A north-light window in the back bedroom where I do my best colour judging
Can hold a swatch up to north light and tell you within a couple of per cent what dyes went into it
Knows the quirks of the old reactive dyes and how acid and pH change a shade between a lab dip and a full batch

projects.name: Clearing out the lab
projects.text: The works closed on the 30th of August. I was allowed back for two days to clear my bench. I took home my notebooks, a set of dyed swatch cards from my first year, a pair of reading glasses I'd lost in 2009, and my lab coat. The rest was skipped by a liquidator's team. I'm now sorting the swatch cards by hue on the dining room table. My wife says the table is not for work. I say it's not work, it's grief. There was a dye-stained apron too, which I took out of the bin and put back three times before finally leaving it. In the end I took the lot of the swatch cards home in a Aldi bag. There are 612 of them, from 1998 to this August, each one with a date, a recipe code and a little pencil mark in the corner if I thought the match was exact. Maybe a hundred and forty of them have the pencil mark. I never told anybody I kept those.

projects.name: The allotment
projects.text: I have a half plot at the back of the Falinge estate. This summer I let it go because of the layoff rumours. Autumn is for digging and putting in garlic. I'm trying to get back into it, because standing in the rain doing something with my hands is better than sitting at the kitchen table doing nothing. The soil's heavy clay. Everything that's planted comes up late. Carol says the leeks are the only things that have ever loved me back. I told her she'd forgotten the dog.

projects.name: Looking for work
projects.text: I've sent out eleven applications since the closure. Three are for lab technician jobs, one for a paint company, one for a textile finisher, and six I don't want to talk about. I've had two replies, both saying thanks but no. The Jobcentre lady was kind and said there's an age bias she's not allowed to mention. Application number twelve is for a part-time role at a school doing art and textiles. The Jobcentre lad says they want a degree. I told him I did a City & Guilds in dyeing at nineteen. He said that probably doesn't count. I said it counted for twenty-eight years.

notes.text: Walked Biscuit up on the Pennine moors, Blackstone Edge. Heather gone brown. Nobody about. I stood at the trig point for a while thinking of the first time I matched a shade, a navy for a school uniform order, 1998. My supervisor said it was good. I was prouder than when my daughter was born, and I've never told anyone that.

The post I put on the old works' Facebook group got forty-odd likes. All I wrote was 'Twenty-eight years and that's that.' Three people messaged me privately, which I wasn't expecting. One of the lads from dyeing said he's driving a bus now. I haven't answered any of them. I don't know what to say.

Rochdale AFC lost 2-0 at home. Sat in the stand with Tom, my brother-in-law. Cold. We talked about the works instead of the match. He said what are you going to do, Den. I said I don't know. He said, you could do anything, you know colours. I said nobody pays for knowing colours anymore.

Walked down to the canal with Biscuit and stood where the old works used to blow its steam every morning at ten to seven. There's a fence now. Behind it, a pile of rubble the colour of old mustard. A man with a clipboard was taking pictures. I asked what they were going to build. He said flats. I said, nobody lives near a dye works for the view. He said that's why they're flats.

Carol has found a flat in Southport. Two bedrooms, a view of the pier if you stand on a chair. She says we could sell up and be there by spring. I haven't said no. I haven't said yes. I said I'd think. I've been thinking in the same circle for a week.

Dreamt about the dye kitchen. Everything was where it should be. The big steel vats, the smell of wet wool, the radio on the shelf playing Radio 2. I woke at four and couldn't get back to sleep. Went downstairs and sat with the swatch cards and my cup of tea, got them half sorted before light.

Gareth came round with a six-pack. We laid the swatch cards out on the dining room table by hue, reds on the left, blues on the right. He picked up a green and said, I remember this one, the Salford Rovers bib order. I said, it's not quite right, it was supposed to be a touch bluer. He said, Den, it was perfect. We stood there for a bit, two grown men holding bits of cardboard.

Went into Debenhams' old building for the Jobcentre session. The lad running it asked me to put my skills into a CV format. I said 'colour matching'. He said 'what's that in transferable terms?' I said 'seeing.' He wrote 'attention to detail'. I hate CVs.

Daughter Hannah rang from Leeds. She says I should put my stuff online, do a YouTube about colour. I said who would watch an old man matching shades. She said you'd be surprised. I told her I'm not that sort of person. She said 'Dad, you're the sort of person who knows things.' I put the phone down gently so she wouldn't hear me nearly cry.

Hannah has sent me a link to a woman in Edinburgh who dyes wool with plants and talks about how hard it is to make the same colour twice. She says madder and woad batches never come out the same, which made me laugh out loud. I could tell her why. I won't, because I don't know her, and who'd listen to a man from Rochdale. But I did say it to the dog.

Dug over half the allotment. Back aching but the soil is good. Found a worm the size of my finger. Put it back. Found myself counting, for no reason, the shades of brown in the soil. I got to eleven before I stopped.

Rang the Jobcentre about the interview for the lab tech job, they said the employer's gone with someone younger. Tom took me for a pint at the Wellington. We said little. He bought the second round without being asked.

messages.text:
Carol: Pork or chicken tonight?
Me: Whatever you fancy.
Carol: That's not an answer, Den.
Me: Chicken then.

Tom: Match on Saturday? I've got the tickets.
Me: Go on then.
Tom: You all right?
Me: Aye. Just tired.

Gareth: Heard you've got swatch cards you saved from the lab. Any chance I could see them?
Me: Aye, any time.
Gareth: I've got nothing to do, honestly.
Me: Me neither. Come Thursday.

Hannah: Dad, I was serious about the video idea.
Me: I know.
Hannah: At least write down what you know. Even if no one reads it.
Me: I'll think about it.

Gareth: Just seen a job at a carpet mill in Bury. Colour technician. Interested?
Me: Depends what they pay.
Gareth: Does it matter?
Me: It matters a bit, Gareth.

Advisor: Mr Whitlock, there's a lab assistant role at a paint company in Salford. Fixed term, six months.
Me: Thank you. Will I need to travel?
Advisor: It's on the tram line.
Me: I'll apply.

Carol: The estate agent rang about the flat. They need an answer by the 15th.
Me: I know.
Carol: Den, I'm not trying to push you out of Rochdale.
Me: I know that too.

calendar.event: Dig and plant garlic at the allotment

relations.about: wife of thirty-one years, wants to move to the coast and is patient but tired of waiting
brother-in-law, football and pints, says little but turns up
daughter in Leeds, thinks I know more than I think
Ex-colleague from the dyeing floor, also laid off; keeps ringing me even when he has nothing to say, which I've come to rely on

constraints: Mortgage nearly paid but redundancy money won't last long
Not keen on moving away from Rochdale
Not comfortable with computers beyond email and Facebook
sensitive: Feels worthless since the works closed
Hasn't told Carol how bad the lack of work feels
Savings and redundancy payout numbers are private
